primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, anointing primarily symbolizes consecration—being set apart by God for a holy office or task—and, closely joined to this, the empowering presence of the Holy Spirit coming upon the person anointed. Kings, priests, and prophets were anointed with oil to mark divine appointment, and the oil is widely read as a type or symbol of the Spirit. This converges in the title 'Messiah/Christ' ('Anointed One'), understood as Jesus being anointed with the Holy Spirit for his saving mission, with believers sharing in that anointing.
primary_basis: Exodus 30:22-33 (sacred anointing oil consecrating priests and tabernacle)
Exodus 29:7; Leviticus 8:12 (anointing of Aaron as priest)
1 Samuel 16:13 (David anointed and the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him)
Isaiah 61:1 ('The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me')
Acts 10:38 ('God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power')
2 Corinthians 1:21-22 (God has anointed us, sealed us, given the Spirit)
1 John 2:20, 27 (believers have an anointing from the Holy One that teaches them)
Psalm 133:2 (anointing oil on Aaron as image of blessing)

alternatives.meaning: Anointing as a sign and means of healing—oil applied to the sick in prayer, formalized in Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions as a sacrament (Anointing of the Sick / Holy Unction) and practiced broadly in Protestant churches.
Anointing as an expression of joy, blessing, honor, and hospitality—festal oil for guests and for gladness, contrasted with mourning.
Anointing for burial and devotion—the anointing of Jesus' body (or in anticipation of his death) as an act of costly love and preparation for burial.

Charismatic/Pentecostal usage of 'the anointing' as a present, sometimes tangible endowment of divine power for ministry, preaching, or miracles, occasionally treated as transferable or yoke-breaking.
basis: Isaiah 10:27 (KJV, 'the yoke shall be destroyed because of the anointing')

alternatives.meaning: Anointing (in 1 John) read specifically as the indwelling word/truth or teaching received at conversion rather than the Spirit per se—a debated exegetical option among commentators.

notes: There is a strong, recognizable consensus that anointing symbolizes divine consecration to office (prophet, priest, king) and the bestowal/empowerment of the Holy Spirit, with the oil widely treated as a symbol of the Spirit; this culminates in the meaning of 'Christ/Messiah' as 'the Anointed One.' The alternative readings listed are not so much rivals as distinct biblical uses of anointing (healing, hospitality/joy, burial) that most interpreters hold alongside the primary symbolic meaning. The main genuinely contested area is the charismatic notion of 'the anointing' as a transferable power-substance, which is criticized by many evangelical and mainline interpreters but is widespread in Pentecostal/charismatic contexts.
